questions.q: State the formula for calculating annual depreciation under Straight Line Method and Written Down Value Method. Identify the key variable that differs in the denominator of each formula.
questions.a: SLM: Annual Depreciation = (Cost - Scrap Value) / Useful Life. WDV: Depreciation = Book Value at Beginning of Year × Rate%. The key difference: SLM denominator is "Useful Life" (constant), WDV applies rate to "Book Value" (diminishes yearly). A wrong answer revealing confusion between "original cost" and "book value" as the base indicates the student hasn't grasped the fundamental distinction in allocation basis.

questions.q: A company purchases a delivery van for ₹10,00,000 with estimated life 5 years, scrap ₹1,00,000. Under SLM, annual depreciation is ₹1,80,000. Under WDV at 30%, Year 1 depreciation is ₹3,00,000. Explain why the WDV charge is higher initially but will be lower in Year 5, and what this implies for profit reporting in early vs. late years.
questions.a: WDV charges 30% on reducing balance: Year 1 = ₹3,00,000 (on ₹10L), Year 5 ≈ ₹72,030 (on ₹2.4L). SLM charges fixed ₹1,80,000 yearly. WDV front-loads expense → lower early profits, higher later profits vs. SLM. A student saying "WDV is always higher" or "profits are same total" misses the timing difference and its impact on profit trends, tax planning, and dividend capacity across years.

questions.q: Asset A (office building) and Asset B (laptop) both cost ₹5,00,000 with 10-year life and ₹50,000 scrap. Repair costs: Building ₹10,000/year constant; Laptop ₹5,000 Year 1, ₹15,000 Year 5, ₹40,000 Year 10. Using the "total charge against P&L (depreciation + repairs)" criterion, determine which method suits each asset and justify with calculated totals for Year 1 and Year 10.
questions.a: Building: SLM dep ₹45,000 + repair ₹10,000 = ₹55,000 constant → suitable. WDV dep Year 1 ₹75,000 (15%) + ₹10,000 = ₹85,000; Year 10 ~₹16,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹26,000 → total charge declines, not matching constant utility. Laptop: WDV Year 1 ₹75,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹80,000; Year 10 ~₹16,000 + ₹40,000 = ₹56,000 → roughly equal total charge. SLM: ₹45,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹50,000 Year 1; ₹45,000 + ₹40,000 = ₹85,000 Year 10 → rising burden. Wrong assignment shows failure to apply the "matching depreciation pattern to repair pattern" principle.

questions.q: The Income Tax Act recognises WDV but not SLM for tax depreciation. A company uses SLM for books (₹2,00,000/year) but must compute tax depreciation under WDV (₹3,50,000 Year 1). Explain the concept of "timing difference" and "deferred tax" that arises, and why this doesn't mean the company pays less tax overall.
questions.a: Year 1: Book dep ₹2L < Tax dep ₹3.5L → taxable profit lower than accounting profit by ₹1.5L → current tax lower, but a deferred tax liability of ₹1.5L × tax rate is created. Over asset life, total dep same (₹depreciable cost), so timing differences reverse. Total tax paid identical; only timing differs. A student claiming "company saves tax permanently" confuses timing difference with permanent difference, missing the reversal mechanism and deferred tax accounting.

questions.q: Critique this statement: "WDV is always better because it's recognised by Income Tax Act and gives higher depreciation in early years, reducing tax." Provide three counter-arguments with specific scenarios where SLM would be preferred.
questions.a: Counter-arguments: (1) SLM suits assets with even utility (leasehold land, patents) where WDV would under-depreciate early and over-depreciate late, distorting profit trends. (2) SLM allows full write-down to zero/scrap; WDV never reaches zero, leaving residual book value requiring adjustment. (3) For companies wanting stable EPS for investor confidence, SLM's constant charge avoids WDV's declining expense pattern. A student unable to name asset-type suitability or the "never reaches zero" limitation shows superficial understanding of method selection criteria.

questions.q: Design a decision flowchart (text-based) that a junior accountant could use to select between SLM and WDV for any new asset. Include at least four decision nodes with yes/no branches, referencing the five NCERT comparison criteria.
questions.a:
Example flowchart:
1. Is asset subject to high technological obsolescence? Yes → WDV; No → Q2.
2. Do repair costs increase significantly over life? Yes → WDV; No → Q3.
3. Is tax depreciation alignment critical (no separate tax computation)? Yes → WDV; No → Q4.
4. Does asset need full write-down to zero/scrap (e.g., leasehold)? Yes → SLV; No → Consider SLM for stable profit reporting.
A poor flowchart using only "asset type" or "management preference" without the five criteria shows inability to operationalise the comparative framework.
